pharm: Naturally occurring weak estrogen used mainly vaginally for urogenital atrophy and orally for menopausal symptoms, acting on estrogen receptors in target tissues.
quick: Vaginal: 0.5 mg cream/pessary daily then taper to 1-2x weekly; oral: 1-2 mg daily (per SmPC)
Oral may be taken with or without food; vaginal at bedtime
Not recommended; estrogens may reduce milk and pass into milk
Use with caution; no specific adjustment established
May influence estrogen metabolism; moderate use
Endometrium with prolonged use, blood pressure, breast exam, VTE risk
summary: Estriol is a naturally occurring, weak, short-acting estrogen (not FDA-approved as a stand-alone drug in the USA; widely used in Europe/Asia per SmPC/BNF). It is used chiefly as a vaginal cream or pessary for atrophic vaginitis and urogenital symptoms of estrogen deficiency, and orally for menopausal complaints. Because it binds the estrogen receptor only briefly, low-dose vaginal estriol has limited systemic and endometrial stimulation, making it a preferred local option for postmenopausal urogenital atrophy. As with all estrogens, it carries class risks including venous thromboembolism, stroke, and (with unopposed systemic use) endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, and is contraindicated in pregnancy, estrogen-dependent cancers, and active thromboembolic disease.
indications: Atrophic vaginitis and urogenital symptoms of estrogen deficiency (vaginal use)
Treatment of menopausal symptoms such as hot flushes (oral use, per SmPC)
Preoperative/postoperative adjunct for atrophic vaginal mucosa (e.g., before vaginal surgery)

dosage.d: 0.5 mg once daily for 2-3 weeks, then reduce to a maintenance dose of 0.5 mg twice weekly
dosage.n: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration; per SmPC

dosage.d: Commonly 1-2 mg daily initially, adjusted to symptoms (per SmPC)
dosage.n: Add a progestogen if the uterus is intact and systemic doses are used long-term

dosage.d: 0.5 mg daily in the 2 weeks before vaginal surgery

admin: Insert vaginal cream/pessary at bedtime for best retention
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration
For an intact uterus on systemic (oral) estrogen, add a progestogen to protect the endometrium
Reassess need for treatment periodically (at least annually)
Take oral tablets at the same time each day
moa: Estriol is an endogenous estrogen that binds estrogen receptors in target tissues (vagina, vulva, urethra, endometrium). Receptor binding promotes maturation and cornification of the vaginal/urogenital epithelium, restores normal vaginal pH and flora, and relieves atrophy-related dryness and dyspareunia. Estriol has a short duration of receptor occupancy and lower potency than estradiol, so at low vaginal doses it exerts mainly local effects with comparatively little systemic or endometrial stimulation.

absolute: Known, past, or suspected breast cancer or other estrogen-dependent malignancy
Active or previous venous thromboembolism (DVT, pulmonary embolism)
Active or recent arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., angina, myocardial infarction, stroke)
Active liver disease or history of liver disease where liver function tests have not normalized
monitor: Endometrial status with prolonged systemic use

preg: Estriol is contraindicated in pregnancy. If pregnancy occurs during treatment, stop immediately; estrogens are not indicated in pregnancy and may pose a risk to the fetus.
lact: Estrogens are not recommended during breastfeeding. They may reduce the quantity and alter the composition of breast milk, and small amounts pass into milk.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established; use with caution in renal impairment as fluid retention may worsen conditions such as hypertension.
hepatic: Contraindicated in active liver disease or where prior hepatic dysfunction has not resolved. Estrogens are metabolized in the liver, and cholestatic jaundice has occurred; discontinue if jaundice or significant LFT abnormalities develop.

major: Enzyme-inducing drugs (rifampicin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St John's wort) - increase estrogen metabolism and reduce efficacy
moderate: Some HIV protease inhibitors and NNRTIs - variably alter estrogen levels
Thyroid hormone - estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, possibly increasing levothyroxine requirements
Corticosteroids - estrogens may increase their effect
minor: Grapefruit juice may modestly increase estrogen levels
interactions.food: Oral form may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Acute alcohol intake may transiently raise circulating estrogen levels; use in moderation.
interactions.diagnostics: Estrogens increase thyroid-binding, cortisol-binding and sex-hormone-binding globulins and can alter coagulation and lipid test results.

monitoring: Endometrium and any abnormal vaginal bleeding (especially with prolonged systemic use)
Breast examination and mammography per screening
counsel: Use the smallest amount that controls your symptoms, for the shortest time needed
For vaginal cream/pessary, insert at bedtime so it stays in place
Report any unexpected vaginal bleeding promptly
Seek urgent help for leg swelling/pain, chest pain, breathlessness, sudden severe headache, or weakness/numbness (clot warning signs)
Attend regular breast and pelvic checks while on estrogen therapy
pk: Local urogenital effect over days to weeks; oral effect on symptoms within weeks
Oral peak plasma concentration within 1-2 hours; vaginal absorption is low at maintenance doses
Short - estriol has a brief plasma half-life (a few hours) and short receptor occupancy
Short-acting; maintenance dosing (often twice weekly vaginally) sustains effect
Store at controlled room temperature; protect from light; keep cream/pessaries as labeled
pearls: NOT a stand-alone FDA-approved drug in the USA - data drawn from European SmPC/BNF; widely used elsewhere for urogenital atrophy
Weak, short-acting estrogen - low-dose vaginal estriol gives mainly local effect with little endometrial stimulation, so a progestogen is generally not required for low-dose vaginal use
Preferred local option for postmenopausal vaginal atrophy and recurrent urinary symptoms
Still carries estrogen class risks: VTE, stroke, and (with systemic unopposed use) endometrial cancer
Estriol rises markedly in pregnancy as a placental product - but exogenous estriol is contraindicated in pregnancy
missed: Vaginal: if you miss a dose, use it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next; do not double up. Oral: take a missed tablet the same day if remembered, otherwise skip it - do not take two together.
overdose: Estrogen overdose typically causes nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness, fluid retention, and withdrawal bleeding in women. Acute toxicity is low; management is supportive and symptomatic, with discontinuation of the product.
